newsitem.title: BELGIUM: UCB running out of steam in Brussels.
newsitem.headline: UCB running out of steam in Brussels.

text.p: Belgian shares, taking their cue from Wall Street's leap overnight, were comfortably higher on Friday despite a lack of support from chemicals and pharmaceuticals firm UCB which finally ran out of steam after having jumped 18 percent in the past two days.
"It doesn't surprise me that UCB went up, but I'm surprised by the speed and the amount, this is exaggerated," one analyst said.
At 0900 GMT, UCB was down 1.1 percent at 118,000 francs after having jumped 2.3 percent to a new record high of 122,000 francs shortly after the opening.

UCB's retreat immediately weighed on the Bel-20 index, which rose 0.82 percent to a record high of 2,410.80 francs shortly after the opening before it was swiftly stripped of all its gains to stand just 0.03 percent, or 0.72 point, up at 2,391.95 by 0905 GMT.
The Bel-20 was still at 1,871.05 points at the start of the year.

Generale Bank said that UCB's rise had been fuelled by the fact it had remained steady for several months at the 95,000 francs level until investors were woken up by comments by UCB CEO Georges Jacobs earlier this week.

Jacobs said that after an increase in ordinary pre-tax profits by 33 percent in 1996 to 5.6 billion francs, UCB was likely to have a similar increase in 1997. That news, together with an announcement that a share split was being considered, propelled the stock and the index to record highs.

Another contributor to the record run was retailer Colruyt, like UCB a market laggard which was suddenly rediscovered earlier this week when players were notified that it would publish full year 1996/1997 earnings on June 26 amid rumours it might sell its Dolmen Computer unit. Colruyt has said it would split Dolmen in two units but had no plans to sell it.
But unlike UCB, Colruyt continued its surge and was up 3.1 percent at an all-time high of 16,750 francs by 0920 GMT, bringing its total gain this week at 15.5 percent.
One analyst played down the potential impact of Dolmen on Colruyt's consolidated profit but noted at the same time that the company often underestimated its own profit.
